_source: Official USCIS Civics Questions and Answers (2008 version), rev. 08/21. PDF page footers, control characters and line wrapping removed; question and answer wording preserved.
_whoTakesThis: Applicants who filed Form N-400 BEFORE 20 October 2025 take this 2008 test. Those filing on or after that date take the 2025 test, which has 128 questions and a different pass mark.
_format: The officer asks up to 10 of the 100 questions orally. Six correct out of ten passes.
_variable: Ten answers depend on location or current officials. The application resolves these from a dated reference snapshot or an answer saved by the learner.

places.name: District of Columbia
places.note: D.C. is not a state. It has no U.S. Senators, no Governor, and no state capital. USCIS accepts those answers.

places.name: Puerto Rico
places.note: A U.S. territory. No U.S. Senators. It has a Governor and a Resident Commissioner rather than a voting Representative.

places.name: Guam
places.note: A U.S. territory. No U.S. Senators. It has a Governor and a nonvoting Delegate.

places.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
places.note: A U.S. territory. No U.S. Senators. It has a Governor and a nonvoting Delegate.

places.name: American Samoa
places.note: A U.S. territory. No U.S. Senators. It has a Governor and a nonvoting Delegate.

places.name: Northern Mariana Islands
places.note: A U.S. territory. No U.S. Senators. It has a Governor and a nonvoting Delegate.

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.hint: Think of the highest legal authority: every other law must agree with it.

questions.q: What does the Constitution do?
questions.hint: The Constitution is the government's rulebook: it creates the structure and protects rights.

questions.q: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
questions.hint: The opening words identify the people as the source of government power. Remember the exact three-word phrase.

questions.q: What is an amendment?
questions.hint: An amendment changes or adds to the Constitution; it does not replace the whole document.

questions.q: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
questions.hint: The first ten amendments form a named group that protects basic rights.

questions.q: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
questions.hint: Think of speaking, worshipping, meeting, publishing, or asking government to act. You only need one freedom.

questions.q: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
questions.hint: Remember 10 + 17: the original Bill of Rights, plus seventeen more amendments.

questions.q: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
answers: said that the United States is free (from Great Britain)
questions.hint: The Declaration explains both independence from Britain and the ideas behind it.

questions.q: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
questions.hint: The famous phrase lists life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Give two of these.

questions.q: What is freedom of religion?
answers: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.
questions.hint: Religious freedom includes choosing a religion or choosing not to practice one.

questions.q: What is the economic system in the United States?
questions.hint: Think of businesses and consumers making choices in a market.

questions.q: What is the “rule of law”?
answers: No one is above the law.
questions.hint: The rule applies to everyone, including the people who run the government.

questions.q: Name one branch or part of the government.
questions.hint: Name one branch: legislative, executive, or judicial. You do not need all three in this version.

questions.q: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
questions.hint: Power is divided so that each branch can check the others.

questions.q: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
questions.hint: “Executive” connects to executing, or carrying out, the laws.

questions.q: Who makes federal laws?
questions.hint: Legislators write laws. The president can then sign or veto a bill.

questions.q: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
questions.hint: Congress has two chambers. You need to name both, not just one.

questions.q: How many U.S. Senators are there?
questions.hint: There are 50 states, and each has two senators: 50 × 2.

questions.q: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
questions.hint: The term pattern is House 2, President 4, Senate 6 years.

questions.q: Who is one of your state’s U.S. Senators now?
answers: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. Senators.]
questions.hint: You only need one of your state's two U.S. senators. Check the state panel before your interview.

questions.q: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
questions.hint: The House has 435 voting seats; the Senate has 100. Keep the two numbers separate.

questions.q: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
questions.hint: House members face voters most often: use the 2–4–6 term pattern.

questions.q: Name your U.S. Representative.
answers: Answers will vary. [Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) Representatives in Congress.]
questions.hint: Your representative depends on your home address and district, not just your state or ZIP code.

questions.q: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
questions.hint: A senator represents the whole state, including people who did not vote for them.

questions.q: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
questions.hint: More people means more House seats. Senate seats stay equal for every state.

questions.q: We elect a President for how many years?
questions.hint: Remember the middle number in House 2, President 4, Senate 6.

questions.q: In what month do we vote for President?
questions.hint: Think of the fall election month, not inauguration month.

questions.q: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the President of the United States.
questions.hint: Use the president serving at your interview, not the president when you filed your application.

questions.q: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.
questions.hint: The vice president is a separate office. Check the current name before your interview.

questions.q: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
questions.hint: Think of the first person in the presidential line of succession.

questions.q: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
questions.hint: After the vice president, the Speaker of the House is next in the presidential line of succession.

questions.q: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
questions.hint: The military's civilian leader is also the head of the executive branch.

questions.q: Who signs bills to become laws?
questions.hint: Congress passes a bill; the president signs it into law.

questions.q: Who vetoes bills?
questions.hint: A veto is the president's rejection of a bill.

questions.q: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
questions.hint: The Cabinet gives advice. It is not a chamber of Congress.

questions.q: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
answers: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
questions.hint: Choose two different job titles, such as Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury. Names are not needed.

questions.q: What does the judicial branch do?
answers: decides if a law goes against the Constitution
questions.hint: Judicial work involves interpreting laws and deciding legal disputes.

questions.q: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.hint: “Supreme” means highest. This court is at the top of the federal court system.

questions.q: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the number of justices on the Supreme Court.
questions.hint: This asks how many justices are serving. Check the current Court; vacancies can change the number.

questions.q: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.
questions.hint: The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court. Verify the current name in the state and officials panel.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
questions.hint: National powers concern the country as a whole, such as money, war, and treaties.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
questions.hint: Think about everyday state services: schools, police, and driver's licenses.

questions.q: Who is the Governor of your state now?
answers: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a Governor.]
questions.hint: A governor leads a state, not the federal government. D.C. has no governor.

questions.q: What is the capital of your state?
answers: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name the capital of the territory.]
questions.hint: Your state capital may not be its biggest city. D.C. is not a state and has no state capital.

questions.q: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
questions.hint: Think of the two main parties, not their current candidates. Name both parties.

questions.q: What is the political party of the President now?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the political party of the President.
questions.hint: Check the current president’s party. It may change with a future president.

questions.q: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
questions.hint: The Speaker leads the House. This person's name can change, so check the linked source.

questions.q: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
answers: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
questions.hint: Choose one voting change: age 18, no poll tax, women's voting rights, or voting regardless of race.

questions.q: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
questions.hint: Think of serving on a jury or voting in a federal election. One is enough.

questions.q: Name one right only for United States citizens.
questions.hint: Think of a federal election: citizens may vote or run for federal office.

questions.q: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
questions.hint: Give two distinct rights. Speech and religion make a useful pair.

questions.q: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
questions.hint: The pledge expresses loyalty to the country and its flag, not to a particular president.

questions.q: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
answers: give up loyalty to other countries
defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
obey the laws of the United States
serve in the U.S. military (if needed)
serve (do important work for) the nation (if needed)
be loyal to the United States
questions.hint: One promise is enough here. Think of obeying U.S. laws or defending the Constitution.

questions.q: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
questions.hint: The Twenty-sixth Amendment lowered the voting age to eighteen.

questions.q: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
answers: give an elected official your opinion on an issue
publicly support or oppose an issue or policy
questions.hint: Pick two actions, such as voting and contacting elected officials.

questions.q: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
questions.hint: The study answer is April 15. Actual filing deadlines can shift for weekends, holidays, or extensions.

questions.q: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
questions.hint: Remember registration begins at 18 and covers ages 18 through 25, before the 26th birthday.

questions.q: What is one reason colonists came to America?
questions.hint: Think about what colonists hoped to find or what they hoped to escape.

questions.q: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
questions.hint: Indigenous peoples lived here long before European arrival.

questions.q: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
questions.hint: Remember that enslaved people were forcibly taken from Africa; this was not voluntary migration.

questions.q: Why did the colonists fight the British?
answers: because of high taxes (taxation without representation)
because the British army stayed in their houses (boarding, quartering)
questions.hint: “Taxation without representation” links taxes to the lack of self-government.

questions.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
questions.hint: Connect Jefferson with the Declaration; connect Madison with the Constitution.

questions.q: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.hint: Think of Independence Day, then add the year 1776.

questions.q: There were 13 original states. Name three.
questions.hint: You need three original states here. New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania form a useful set.

questions.q: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
answers: The Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.
questions.hint: The event is named for the document the delegates wrote there.

questions.q: When was the Constitution written?
questions.hint: Separate the dates: Declaration in 1776, Constitution in 1787.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
questions.hint: Remember the initials H, M, J: Hamilton, Madison, Jay. Only one writer is needed.

questions.q: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
answers: oldest member of the Constitutional Convention
first Postmaster General of the United States
questions.hint: Pick one of Franklin's public contributions, such as libraries or the postal service.

questions.q: Who is the “Father of Our Country”?
questions.hint: Washington is associated with several “firsts,” including the first presidency.

questions.q: Who was the first President?
questions.hint: Washington is associated with several “firsts,” including the first presidency.

questions.q: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
questions.hint: Think of the Louisiana Purchase. It covered much more than today's state of Louisiana.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
questions.hint: Choose a war in the nineteenth century. The Civil War is one accepted answer.

questions.q: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
questions.hint: A civil war is a conflict within one country. Here, it was between North and South.

questions.q: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
questions.hint: Slavery was central to the conflict. It is one of the accepted answers in this question.

questions.q: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
answers: led the United States during the Civil War
questions.hint: Link Lincoln to the Civil War, preserving the Union, and the Emancipation Proclamation.

questions.q: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
answers: freed slaves in the Confederate states
freed slaves in most Southern states
questions.hint: The proclamation declared freedom for enslaved people in Confederate areas; it did not immediately end all slavery nationwide.

questions.q: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
questions.hint: Susan B. Anthony worked for women’s rights, including the right to vote.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
questions.hint: Both world wars took place in the twentieth century. Either is an accepted example.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Who was President during World War I?
questions.hint: Link World War I with Woodrow Wilson: both begin with W.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
questions.hint: Think FDR, not Theodore Roosevelt. Franklin Roosevelt served during both events.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
questions.hint: Name all three Axis countries listed: Japan, Germany, and Italy.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
questions.hint: Eisenhower was a general before becoming president. World War II is one useful connection.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
questions.hint: Distinguish the concern from the rival: communism or nuclear war, rather than the name of a country.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
questions.hint: Focus on ending unequal treatment based on race.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
answers: worked for equality for all Americans
questions.hint: Connect Dr. King with civil rights and equality for all Americans.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: What major event happened on September 11, 2001, in the United States?
questions.hint: “9/11” refers to the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001.

questions.topic: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.q: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States. [USCIS Officers will be supplied with a list of federally recognized American Indian tribes.]
questions.hint: Choose one tribe and practice its name. Cherokee or Navajo are accepted examples.

questions.q: Name one of the two longest rivers in the United States.
questions.hint: Both accepted river names start with M. You only need one.

questions.q: What ocean is on the West Coast of the United States?
questions.hint: Think west toward California and the Pacific.

questions.q: What ocean is on the East Coast of the United States?
questions.hint: Think east toward the Atlantic and Europe.

questions.q: Name one U.S. territory.
questions.hint: A territory is not a state. Puerto Rico or Guam is one accepted example.

questions.q: Name one state that borders Canada.
questions.hint: Think of the northern border. Alaska also borders Canada.

questions.q: Name one state that borders Mexico.
questions.hint: Trace the southern border west to east: California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas.

questions.q: What is the capital of the United States?
questions.hint: Distinguish the national capital from your own state capital.

questions.q: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
answers: Liberty Island [Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).]
questions.hint: Think of New York Harbor and Liberty Island.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
answers: because the stripes represent the original colonies
questions.hint: Stripes look back to the original colonies; stars represent today's states.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
answers: because there is one star for each state
because each star represents a state
questions.hint: One star stands for each state. Compare this with the thirteen stripes.

questions.q: What is the name of the national anthem?
questions.hint: The anthem's name refers to the flag. It is different from the Pledge of Allegiance.

questions.q: When do we celebrate Independence Day?
questions.hint: This holiday celebrates independence from Britain. The date is July 4.

questions.q: Name two national U.S. holidays.
questions.hint: You need two national holidays in this version. Independence Day and Thanksgiving are a useful pair.
